answers.why: With an empty outbox the mutant skips the early return, adds the empty array to the private WeakSet `projected`, and runs the loop zero times, so it returns the same `events` as the original. The only extra effect is a WeakSet entry for an empty array, and that entry can never change output: an empty outbox reports nothing whether or not it is in the set. A WeakSet can't be counted or listed from outside, so no test can see the difference.

rounds.reply:
I added one test for M1. M2 is equivalent to the real code, so no test can catch it. Both tests in the file pass, and the original promise check is unchanged.

**M1** (`state.lifecycle ?? []` becomes `["Stryker was here"]`): no test ever gave the projector a state without a `lifecycle` field, which is what a state saved before the outbox existed looks like. With the mutant, that fallback becomes one string "note". The string has no `kind`, so the switch in `projectNote` matches no case and returns `undefined`. The check `event !== null` lets `undefined` through, so the projector would return `[undefined]` instead of `[]`. The new test starts a run, removes `lifecycle` from the state, and checks that projecting both a host Msg and the agent's Msg gives exactly `[]`. I used `toStrictEqual` so an array holding `undefined` can't count as equal to an empty one.

**M2** (`outbox.length === 0 || …` becomes `false || …`): for an empty outbox, the mutant skips the early return. It then adds that empty array to `projected` (a `WeakSet`) and runs the loop zero times. Either way the projector returns the same `events`. The only side effect is the array being in the `WeakSet`, and an empty outbox gives nothing to report whether it's in there or not. A `WeakSet` also can't be counted or listed from outside.

I added three tests to `packages/tea/src/otel/span-time.promise.test.ts`, and each of the four mutants now has a test that should kill it. All 4 tests in the file pass on the current code. I didn't run the mutants: the rules don't allow changing source files, so the kills are worked out from the code.

The original property test is unchanged.

Before writing them I confirmed one thing: the OTel SDK passes an `HrTime` through unchanged. Given `startTime: [0, 1e9]`, the exported span still reads `[0, 1000000000]`. So a wrong `spanTime` result shows up in the exported spans and can be caught.

- **M2 and M3 (the rounding carry at `index.ts:347`):** an `at` of `999.9999999` rounds to exactly 1e9 nanoseconds. The real code turns that into `[1, 0]`. With M2 the span would get `[0, 1000000000]`; with M3 it would get `[-1, 0]`. A second value, `1_999.9999999`, should give `[2, 0]` for the run span's end. The test also checks that every span's nanoseconds stay below 1e9. I kept to small values here because large epoch values can't hold this sub-millisecond detail in a JavaScript number.
- **M1 (`index.ts:229`):** a `TurnSettled` with no `BrainStarted` before it must still produce a `chat` span whose kind is `SpanKind.CLIENT`. With the mutant, the span falls back to the SDK default, `INTERNAL`.
- **M4 (`index.ts:394`):** a brain span and a tool span still open at a `done` `RunDone` must end at the `RunDone`'s `at` (30), without `tea.run.detached`. With the mutant, nothing ends them at that point. The final `end()` call never runs in this test, so the children are never exported and the lookups fail.

I added nine tests per client (18 in all) to `packages/structure-sweep/test/jev-key.promise.test.ts`. All 22 tests in the file pass on this code, and the original promise checks are unchanged. Both `src/jev.ts` files are byte-identical, so each test runs once per client and kills the matching mutant in both packages.

Why each mutant dies, judging from the code (I didn't run any mutants, as the rules say):
- **M1/M2, M12/M13** (empty parts kept): a 401 body of `{error:{message:"", code:"invalid_key"}}` gives detail `"invalid_key"`. Under either mutant the empty message is kept, so the detail becomes `"; invalid_key"`.
- **M3/M14** (always join): when message and code are both empty, the real code leaves detail `undefined`; the mutant gives `""`.
- **M4/M5, M15/M16** (empty-key guard): with an empty key, the real code returns the body untouched. The mutants call `replaceAll("", "[redacted]")`, which inserts `[redacted]` between every character. M5/M16 are also killed by a key that is literally `"Stryker was here!"`: the real code redacts it, the mutant leaves it.
- **M6/M17** (array items become `undefined`): the redacted body must equal the expected structure exactly, including `["plain", "[redacted]", 7, ["x[redacted]y"]]`.
- **M7/M18** (object key replaced with `""`): the body key `k_<key>` must come back as `k_[redacted]`, not `k_`.
- **M8/M19**: a 500 response whose body isn't JSON must read as `{}`, not `undefined`.
- **M9/M20**: a 200 body that echoes the key is passed through unchanged, so redacting success bodies too would fail.
- **M10/M21**: a failing reply with status 200 (the answers don't decode) or 302 (counted as terminal) has an error-shaped body. The real code leaves detail `undefined`; under the mutant it would read `"looks like an error"`.
- **M11/M22**: at exactly status 400, the real code sets the detail to `"bad request"`; with `> 400` it would be `undefined`.
